items.followUp: A force of 150 N acts perpendicular to a spanner 0.30 m from its pivot. Find the torque.

rubric.why: Identifies the equivalence between the pascal and the SI pressure unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equivalence.

rubric.why: Defines one pascal in terms of force and area.
rubric.description: Define 1 Pa as the pressure produced by a perpendicular force of 1 N acting on an area of 1 m².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition, including the force and area.

modelAnswer: Yes, 1 N m⁻² = 1 Pa.
One pascal is the pressure produced when a perpendicular force of 1 N acts on an area of 1 m².

items.followUp: Explain why water rises through a straw when a person sucks air from it.

rubric.why: Recognises that sucking lowers the air pressure in the straw and mouth.
rubric.description: Explain that sucking reduces the pressure inside the straw.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the pressure inside is reduced.

rubric.why: Identifies atmospheric pressure as the force that raises the liquid.
rubric.description: Explain that atmospheric pressure on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up the straw.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role of atmospheric pressure in pushing the liquid upward.

modelAnswer: When we suck air from the straw, the pressure inside the straw becomes lower than atmospheric pressure.
Atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up the straw and into the mouth.

items.followUp: A perpendicular force of 120 N is applied to a wrench 25 cm from its pivot. Find the torque and state its direction if the force acts upward at the left end.

rubric.why: Uses the perpendicular distance from the pivot in metres.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct SI distance.

rubric.why: Applies the torque relation and obtains the magnitude and direction.
rubric.description: Calculate torque as 200 N × 0.20 m = 40 N m; state clockwise.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct torque magnitude with unit and direction.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 200 N; perpendicular distance, d = 20 cm = 0.20 m.
Formula: τ = Fd.
Substitution: τ = 200 N × 0.20 m = 40 N m.
The torque is 40 N m, clockwise about the pivot.

items.followUp: Define equilibrium and give an example of a body in static equilibrium.

rubric.why: States the defining condition for equilibrium in this context.
rubric.description: Define equilibrium as the state in which the resultant force on a body is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the zero-resultant-force condition.

rubric.why: Gives an example of a moving body whose motion is unchanged and whose resultant force is zero.
rubric.description: Give a moving body in dynamic equilibrium, such as a car moving in a straight line at constant velocity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable moving-body example.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
A car moving in a straight line at constant velocity is an example of a moving body in equilibrium.

items.followUp: Find the gravitational potential energy of a 4 kg body raised 8 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Identifies the given quantities in SI units and uses the standard gravitational acceleration assumed for this calculation.
rubric.description: State m = 10 kg, h = 5 m, and g = 10 m s⁻².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly stated data.

rubric.why: Uses gravitational potential energy correctly and evaluates it with the correct unit.
rubric.description: Calculate GPE = mgh = 10 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m = 500 J.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct substitution and answer with unit.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 10 kg; h = 5 m; g = 10 m s⁻².
Formula: GPE = mgh.
Substitution: GPE = 10 kg × 10 m s⁻² × 5 m.
Answer: GPE = 500 J.

items.followUp: What is the SI unit of energy? Define one joule.

rubric.why: Names the SI unit of power.
rubric.description: State that the SI unit of power is the watt (W).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct unit.

rubric.why: Defines power as work done per unit time and relates the definition to the watt.
rubric.description: Define one watt as one joule of work done per second.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

modelAnswer: The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
One watt is the power of a body that does 1 J of work in 1 s; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.

items.followUp: State the law of conservation of momentum and show, using a collision between two bodies, that total momentum is conserved.

rubric.description: State that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if no external force acts on it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law, including the isolated-system condition or equivalent.

rubric.why: Uses equal and opposite interaction forces for the two colliding bodies.
rubric.description: Apply Newton’s third law: the forces during the collision are equal and opposite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct force relationship.

rubric.why: Derives the before-and-after momentum equation from the forces acting during the collision.
rubric.description: Show that the collision gives m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct momentum equation or a valid derivation leading to it.

rubric.why: Verifies the law with a concrete collision example.
rubric.description: Give a consistent example showing equal total momentum before and after collision.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct numerical verification.

modelAnswer: Law: If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
Consider two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ colliding; let their velocities before collision be u₁ and u₂ and after collision be v₁ and v₂.
During the collision, F₁ = m₁(v₁ − u₁)/t and F₂ = m₂(v₂ − u₂)/t.
By Newton’s third law, F₁ = −F₂.
Therefore, m₁(v₁ − u₁) = −m₂(v₂ − u₂), so m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Example: let m₁ = 2 kg, u₁ = 3 m s⁻¹, m₂ = 1 kg, and u₂ = 0; after collision let v₁ = 1 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Momentum before = (2 × 3) + (1 × 0) = 6 kg m s⁻¹; momentum after = (2 × 1) + (1 × 4) = 6 kg m s⁻¹.
Thus, total momentum before the collision equals total momentum after it.
